client: I've been having a really hard time since my brother passed away six months ago — it was a car accident, totally sudden, and I just haven't been the same since. Like, my friends keep inviting me out and I go sometimes, but I just sit there feeling completely hollow, like I'm watching everyone else have fun through a glass wall. I honestly don't know if talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd try because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: What you're carrying right now — the sudden loss of your brother, that hollow feeling even when you're surrounded by people — is an incredibly heavy kind of grief, and the way you're speaking, even with such urgency and speed, hints at how much pain is pressing against you right now. That sense of watching life through a glass wall is such a real and common response to traumatic loss, and it makes complete sense that you haven't felt like yourself. I'm really glad you reached out, and I want you to know that while talking won't undo what happened, it can gently help us understand what you're going through and find small ways to feel less alone in it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I appreciate you saying that, but honestly part of me is already wondering if this is just going to be me talking and talking and nothing actually shifting. I guess I'm just scared this is going to be another thing that doesn't work.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense, and I want to be honest with you — you're right that feeling understood in a session doesn't automatically fill that hollow feeling at 2am, and I'd rather we name that directly than pretend otherwise. What I hear underneath your words, and even in the urgency and intensity in your voice right now, is someone who has already tried to push through this and is exhausted by things that only scratch the surface. So instead of just validating how you feel, I want us to actually work together on *why* that hollowness keeps showing up and what thoughts are driving it — because that's where real change tends to happen.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: Okay, that actually... lands a little differently than I expected. I guess I can try to think about what's driving it, but I'm not even sure I know how to answer that — like when I try to look directly at why I feel hollow, my mind just kind of goes blank or I start thinking about the last conversation I had with my brother and whether I should have called him more. And then I just feel guilty on top of everything else, which makes it worse.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — the "should have called more" — is one of grief's cruelest tricks, and I notice even as you're speaking about it there's something fragile and quietly painful in your voice, like you're carrying this very carefully. Here's something worth gently examining together: the fact that you *remember* that last conversation, that you *care* this deeply, actually speaks to how much love was there — but grief often hijacks that love and turns it into evidence against yourself. That's not truth, that's a thought pattern we can work with.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and some part of me wants to believe that — that the guilt is just a trick my brain is playing. But it's hard to just reframe it as "that's not truth" because it literally is true that I didn't call him as much as I could have in the last few months, we were both just busy and I kept thinking there was more time. So it doesn't feel like a distortion, it feels like a fact I have to live with.
therapist: You're absolutely right, and I don't want to minimize that — it *is* a fact that you didn't call as much, and grief deserves more respect than a quick reframe, so let's sit with that honestly. But here's the question worth turning over slowly: does that fact mean what the guilt is *telling* you it means — that you were a bad brother, that you didn't love him enough? Because I can hear in your voice right now, the intensity, the urgency, how much this matters to you, and that itself is evidence that the story guilt is writing about you may not be the whole truth. The fact that you were both busy, both assuming there was more time — that's a very human thing, not a verdict on who you were to him.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I guess when you put it that way, the guilt being a "verdict" on who I was to him... that hits something. Because I don't actually think I was a bad brother — we were close, we just both got caught up in life, and I think he knew I loved him. But it's like even when I can logically see that, there's still this part of me that won't let go of it, that keeps circling back to those missed calls like it's looking for something to punish me with.
therapist: What you just said is really important — you *know* you weren't a bad brother, and yet something keeps circling back to punish you anyway, and I notice even in the softness and quickness of your voice right now, there's something that sounds almost like you're holding your breath around this. That relentless circling isn't guilt trying to help you do better — it's grief looking for a place to put the unbearable fact that he's gone, and punishing yourself can feel like a way of staying connected to him, like if you let go of the guilt you're somehow letting go of him too. Does that resonate at all?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That actually stopped me for a second because I hadn't thought about it that way — like the guilt is a weird form of holding onto him. But it also scares me a little, because if that's true, then working through the guilt means... what, moving on? And I don't want to move on, that feels like a betrayal, like I'd just be going back to my normal life as if he never existed.
therapist: The fear in your voice right now — soft but racing, like something tender and urgent at the same time — tells me this just touched something really core for you, and I want to gently offer a different way to hold it: working through grief doesn't mean moving on *from* him, it means learning to carry him *with* you differently. He doesn't disappear when the guilt lifts — what you're really afraid of losing is the connection, and that connection lives in your love for him, your memories, who you became because he was your brother, none of which goes anywhere. "Moving on" is the wrong frame; what we're really talking about is finding a way to let him matter without it destroying you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That phrase — "let him matter without it destroying you" — I think I need to sit with that because it's the first thing in six months that hasn't felt like it was asking me to shrink what I'm feeling. But I'm also honest enough to say I don't really know what "carrying him differently" looks like in practice, like when I'm alone at night and it hits me that I can't just pick up the phone and call him, what am I actually supposed to do with that?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, pitched high, like something is pressing to get out — tells me those nighttime moments are very real and very raw, not abstract at all, and I don't want to give you a technique that feels hollow against something that heavy. But here's one small, practical place to start: instead of reaching for the phone and hitting that wall of silence, what if you *did* talk to him — wrote it down, said it out loud, whatever feels less strange — not because it's magic, but because the impulse to reach out is love, and love needs somewhere to go. We can build on what that looks like for you specifically, because "carrying him differently" should feel like *you*, not a grief workbook exercise.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I've actually tried something like that once — I started typing a message to his number on my phone before I even realized what I was doing, and then I just stared at it and couldn't send it and deleted the whole thing because it felt too strange and sad at the same time. I guess what worries me about doing it intentionally is that it might just make the absence feel louder, like I'm reminding myself over and over that there's no one on the other end. But I also hear what you're saying about the love needing somewhere to go, so I don't know, maybe the problem was that I was trying to send it rather than just... letting it exist somewhere.
therapist: What you just figured out in real time — that the problem wasn't reaching out to him, it was the expectation of a response — that's actually a really significant insight, and I can hear in your voice, fast and high and pressing forward, like part of you is working something out even as you speak. That message you typed and deleted didn't need to be sent to be real; it existed, the love in it existed, and maybe the next time that impulse comes you let it live somewhere — a note, a voice memo, even just unsent — not as a reminder that he's gone, but as proof that the connection still is. You just rewrote the exercise yourself, and that matters.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, loud, urgent — even as you're describing something that actually shifted for you, tells me your mind is already racing ahead to the next hard moment, which is itself a kind of anxiety worth noticing gently. So here's something concrete: when the spiral comes before you can think, the goal isn't to reach for insight — it's just to reach for *one small anchor*, something physical and immediate like your feet on the floor, a light on, even just saying out loud "this is grief, it will peak and it will pass." We're essentially building a tiny bridge to get you from overwhelmed back to the version of you who *can* reach for something healthier, and we can keep making that bridge more specific to you as we go.

The goal is that in the spiral, you're not reciting a coping statement, you're actually briefly *with him* — which is exactly what you said you needed.
